title: MUSE stellar kinematics give the ASASSN-14ko black hole about 10^7.35 solar masses, not 10^9, so a light-travel clock needs a 2 percent tail mass; ALMA finds a fading steep-spectrum nuclear core
abstract: Question: proposed clocks for the stalled and resumed period decrease of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko need very different black-hole masses: a light-travel (Roemer) clock needs log M >= 8.19, a precessing star-disc drag clock needs log M <= 7.86-7.98. Published masses disagree (7.86 from host scaling; 9.05 from a MUSE velocity dispersion). Approach: we fitted the stellar spectra of the public MUSE cube of ESO 253-G003 (2015) with pPXF, using the Ca II triplet, masks for the broad AGN lines, regional spectra and a 92-bin Voronoi map; we converted sigma to M with M-sigma relations and reweighted published clock likelihood profiles. We also analysed three public ALMA epochs (2023-2024) of the two nuclei. Results: outside the AGN core the host of the flaring nucleus N has sigma = 98 +/- 6 km/s (Ca II triplet; other N regions 100-132 km/s); the companion S has 146 +/- 7 km/s. A template-only fit of the AGN-dominated nuclear spectrum gives 267-279 km/s, which reproduces the published 10^9.05; masking the broad lines gives 139-157 km/s. With six region choices and Kormendy and Ho (2013), log M(N) = 7.35 +/- 0.42 (95 percent 6.54-8.15); log M = 9.05 has probability 3e-6. The Roemer clock needs a mass with probability 2 percent; its penalised likelihood ratio against a constant period derivative falls from 10^3.2 (host-scaling prior) to 10^2.3. The precessing drag clock is permitted (P = 0.89) but still needs a star of about 10-50 Rsun. ALMA shows a compact (< 25 pc) core at N with 3.5 mJy at 104 GHz and a same-epoch index of -1.06 +/- 0.08 (optically thin synchrotron), 2.5-3.8 dex above the coronal mm/X-ray relation; S lies on that relation. The 229 GHz core of N faded to 0.69 +/- 0.10 of its 2023 level in nine months. Limitations: one MUSE epoch with 0.8 arcsec seeing in a late-stage merger; region choice dominates the error; M-sigma relations are not calibrated for mergers; clock profiles are reused, not refitted; ALMA variability rests on two epochs at different resolution.

display.caption: Black-hole mass of the ASASSN-14ko nucleus from MUSE stellar kinematics (blue) and of the companion nucleus (violet), with published values and the masses that two clocks need; middle and bottom: published clock likelihood profiles against mass.

MUSE stellar kinematics: dispersion map, Ca II triplet fit of the host, the AGN-dominated nuclear spectrum, and dispersion by region and fit set-up; the 10^9.05 value arises from a template-only fit of the nucleus.

ALMA: compact steep-spectrum millimetre core at the flaring nucleus, its fading between 2023 and 2024 at matched resolution, its excess over the coronal mm/X-ray relation, and CO(2-1) gas at both nuclei.

citations.reason: We reweight its Roemer-clock likelihood profile with the dynamical mass; the clock needs a mass with 2 percent probability.
Fixed-mass profile of the disc-crossing clock evaluated at our mass; we show that its high-mass MUSE reference value is an AGN artefact.
Precessing drag clock: its mass requirement is consistent with our dynamical mass; we derive the stellar radius it needs.
Identification of N and S and X-ray luminosities; ALMA confirms S as an AGN on the coronal mm/X-ray relation.
Constant X-ray clock used to phase the ALMA epochs.
Energy budget at 1e7 solar masses, near our median mass.
Pursiainen et al. 2025: MUSE M-sigma mass 10^9.05 for ASASSN-14ko; we reproduce it as an AGN-contamination artefact.
